# Results — Study 272 (Champagne-Index) on the ^GSPC price index

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). Worldwide champagne
shipments are hardcoded in [`data.py`](../champagne_index/data.py) (CIVC figures,
1999–2024). S&P 500 returns are ^GSPC December/December calendar-year **price**
returns from the repo-level cache (`_cache/^GSPC_split_only.parquet`). Match the
fingerprint below to confirm you hold the same data. As-of **2026-06-17**.*

## Data stamp

| Source | Window | n observations | Fingerprint |
|---|---|---|---|
| ^GSPC (price-only, December/December) | forward returns 2001–2025 | 25 forward years | `af1f8d03f90b` |
| Champagne shipments (CIVC) | 1999–2024 (24 growths used) | hardcoded constant | — |

**Alignment (no look-ahead).** The CIVC publishes year *Y*'s shipment total in
January *Y+1*. We use the **forward** convention: champagne YoY growth over year
*Y* is paired with the S&P **price return for year Y+1**. This bakes a one-year
execution lag into the join and is the only tradable specification. A
`contemporaneous` convention is also exposed in `data.py` (slope ≈ +0.01,
corr ≈ +0.05, HAC t ≈ +0.38 — a non-event) purely to show that the label choice
is a degrees-of-freedom decision.

## The unconditional base rate

The S&P 500 (price-only) rose in **72.0%** of the 25 forward years in the sample.
Any "predict up/down" framing must beat this base rate, not a 50% coin.

## Predictive regression (the primary, robust test)

`sp500_return(Y+1) = a + b · z(champagne_growth(Y)) + u`, where `z` is the
standardized YoY champagne growth.

| Quantity | Value |
|---|--:|
| slope `b` (per 1 sd of champagne growth) | **−0.0561** |
| correlation | **−0.326** |
| R² | 0.106 |
| naive OLS t (slope) | −1.652 |
| **HAC (Newey-West) t (slope)** | **−1.296** (lags = 2) |

The slope is **negative** — the folklore direction (more bubbly this year → weaker
market next year) — and the correlation is −0.33. But the robust Newey-West t-stat
is **−1.30**, comfortably inside the noise band. **REAL requires |t_HAC| ≥ 2; this
fails.** The naive OLS t (−1.65) looks a touch stronger, which is exactly why the
HAC correction matters: it removes spurious precision from autocorrelated annual data.

## Contrarian tercile spread (the headline-grabbing, fragile statistic)

| Arm | mean next-year S&P return |
|---|--:|
| After **low** champagne growth (gloom third) | **+18.6%** |
| After **high** champagne growth (party third) | **−2.9%** |
| **Spread (low − high)** | **+21.5pp** |

This split looks spectacular, and its one-sided permutation p-value is **0.0035**.
But it is a tercile statistic on n = 25: it throws away the middle third and is
dominated by a handful of crisis years (2007 boom → 2008 −38.5%; 2021 record →
2022 −19.4%; 2008/2020 gloom → 2009/2021 rebounds). When the robust slope test
(two-sided permutation p = **0.117**) and the headline split disagree, trust the
robust test.

## Permutation tests (10,000 shuffles)

| Statistic | observed | permutation p |
|---|--:|--:|
| OLS slope | −0.056 | 0.117 (two-sided) |
| Tercile spread | +21.5pp | 0.0035 (one-sided) |

## Leave-one-out robustness

Dropping any single year leaves the correlation in the range **[−0.56, −0.17]** —
always negative. So the tilt is **sign-stable**, not one lucky year. That is what
earns a **Weak** rather than a flat **None**. But sign-stability is not
significance: |t_HAC| is still 1.30.

## The n = 25 problem

With 25 forward years, the minimum detectable |correlation| at 80% power
(two-sided, α = 0.05, Fisher-z approximation) is ≈ **0.52**. The observed |corr|
is 0.33 — **below** the detectable threshold. The sample is simply too thin to
confirm an effect of this size, even though the direction is consistent.

## Could you trade it?

Long S&P after below-median champagne growth, short after above-median; one-way
cost 10 bps, short-borrow 50 bps on NAV, executed with the one-year publication lag.

| Strategy | annualised (price-only) |
|---|--:|
| Champagne long/short, gross | +5.1% |
| Champagne long/short, **net** | **+4.7%** |
| Buy & hold ^GSPC | **+6.8%** |
| Net shortfall vs buy-and-hold | **−2.1pp/yr** |

Even gross of costs the overlay barely matches buy-and-hold; net of borrow and
trading costs it loses. Shorting equities in "party" years fights their upward
drift. Note ^GSPC is **price-only** — total return would lift the long-only
benchmark further, *widening* the gap. (Survivorship: the S&P 500 is a
committee-managed index that drops failures; the long-only benchmark is itself an
upper bound.)

## Verdict

- **Signal — WEAK.** Slope negative (corr −0.33), sign-stable under leave-one-out,
  literature-supported direction — but HAC t = −1.30 (< 2) and two-sided
  permutation p = 0.117. It points the right way and whispers, but does not clear
  the |t| ≥ 2 bar. Price-only and survivorship are named here.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** The long/short overlay nets +4.7%/yr vs +6.8%/yr for
  buy-and-hold; shorting equities fights their drift and costs + borrow finish the
  job. There is no tradable edge.
- **Mostly busted.** The marquee hits (2007→2008, 2021→2022) are real and
  seductive, but n = 25 and a couple of dominant years are how mirages are born.
